title: Ma and Pa - Expanding Your Range
description: Add Ma and Pa to your vocabulary, play the first five notes, and start hearing the pentatonic scale.

tasks.title: Meet Ma - the fourth note
content: Ma (Madhyam) means 'the middle one' - it sits right at the centre of the saptak. To play Ma on the bansuri, lift three bottom fingers while keeping the top three closed.

items: Ma - lift 3 bottom fingers (only the top 3 remain closed)

content.text: Ma is the boundary between the lower and upper halves of the scale. In many ragas, Ma defines the mood - shuddha Ma feels calm, tivra Ma feels tense.

questions.prompt: How many bottom fingers do you lift to play Ma?

options.why: One bottom finger gives you Re.
Two bottom fingers gives you Ga.

options.yes: Correct! Three bottom fingers lifted, three top fingers closed.

options.why: All fingers lifted would overblow to the upper octave.

questions.no: Madhyam means 'the middle one' - Ma sits at the centre of the seven notes.

hints: Ma is the fourth of seven notes - right in the middle.
Madhyam shares its root with 'middle'.

tasks.title: Hold Ma steady
content: With three holes open, Ma needs slightly more air support than the lower notes. Keep your breath steady and your embouchure relaxed.
Hold Ma for 4 seconds without the pitch drifting.
hints: If the pitch wavers, you may be using too much air. Ease back slightly.
Make sure the three closed fingers are sealing their holes completely - even a tiny leak sharpens the note.
Keep your jaw and throat relaxed. Tension travels into the sound.

tasks.title: Meet Pa - the fifth note
content: Pa (Pancham) means 'the fifth'. Like Sa, Pa is an 'achal' (immovable) swara - it never changes in any raga.
To play Pa, lift four bottom fingers. Only the top two remain closed.

content.text: The interval from Sa to Pa (a perfect fifth) is the strongest consonance in music. When you play Pa over a Sa drone, you will hear them lock together.

questions.prompt: Pa is special because it is an 'achal' swara. What does that mean?

options.why: Volume depends on breath, not the note.

options.text: It never has a komal or tivra form
options.yes: Correct! Like Sa, Pa is immovable - it has only one form.

options.text: It can only be played in one octave
It must always be played last
options.why: Pa can appear anywhere in a phrase.

hints: Only two notes are 'achal' (immovable) - Sa and Pa.

tasks.title: Hold Pa steady
content: Pa requires even more air support. With four holes open, the air column is shorter and the note wants to jump up. Stay gentle.
hints: If the note squeaks or jumps up, you are blowing too hard. Back off the air pressure.
Think of blowing gently across a bottle top - just enough to make it sing.
Check that the two closed fingers are fully covering their holes.

tasks.title: Fingering quiz
content: Let's make sure you know the fingering for all five notes before playing them together.

questions.prompt: To go from Ga to Ma, what do you do?

options.yes: Right! Each ascending note lifts one more finger from the bottom.

options.why: Ascending means opening more holes, not closing them.
Blowing harder overblows to the upper octave - the fingering changes the note.

questions.prompt: How many finger holes are OPEN when you play Pa?
questions.no: Pa has four holes open and two closed (the top two).

questions.prompt: If you are playing Pa and you close one finger (the third from top), which note do you get?

options.yes: Correct! Closing one hole from Pa brings you back down to Ma.

options.why: Dha is above Pa - you would need to open another hole.

hints: Count from the bottom: 0 open = Sa, 1 open = Re, 2 open = Ga, 3 open = Ma, 4 open = Pa.
Going down reverses the pattern: close fingers from bottom to top.

tasks.title: Ear training - five notes
content: Now that you know all five notes, train your ear to tell them apart. You will hear one note at a time - identify which one.
hints: Sa (lowest) and Pa (highest) are the easiest to spot - listen for the extremes first.
Ma and Ga are close together. Ma sounds slightly more serious; Ga is brighter.
Re sits between Sa and Ga - it has a gentle, calm quality.

tasks.title: Play the ascending scale
content: Play all five notes going up: Sa, Re, Ga, Ma, Pa. One note at a time, clearly and steadily.

questions.prompt: Play Sa Re Ga Ma Pa (ascending).

hints: Go slowly. Each note should ring clearly before you move to the next.
If a note sounds muddy, pause and check your finger positions.
Breathe out steadily - do not speed up or slow down the air.

tasks.title: Play the descending scale
content: Now come back down: Pa, Ma, Ga, Re, Sa. Descending is harder because closing fingers takes more precision than opening them.

questions.prompt: Play Pa Ma Ga Re Sa (descending).

hints: Press each finger down firmly as you descend - air leaks cause squeaks.
Descending often feels less natural. Practice this direction more than ascending.
Think of placing each finger like pressing a piano key - definite and clean.

tasks.title: A simple five-note tune
content: Here is your first tune using all five notes. It goes up, pauses on Pa, then comes back down:
Sa Re Ga Ma Pa - Pa Ma Ga Re Sa

content.text: This ascending-descending pattern is called an 'aaroha-avroha' and is the backbone of every raga.

questions.prompt: Play Sa Re Ga Ma Pa (ascending half).
Play Pa Ma Ga Re Sa (descending half).

hints: Break it in half if needed - master the ascent, then the descent, then connect them.
The aaroha-avroha is the most fundamental melodic pattern in Indian music. This one exercise trains everything.

tasks.title: Final challenge - pentatonic phrase
content: Play this melodic phrase that skips between notes instead of going step by step:
Sa Ga Pa Ga Re Sa
This kind of leap is common in real melodies and tests both your ear and your fingers.

content.text: These five notes (Sa Re Ga Ma Pa) form a pentatonic scale - the same five-note pattern found in folk music around the world.

questions.prompt: Play the phrase: Sa Ga Pa Ga Re Sa.
What is the name for the ascending pattern of notes in a raga?
questions.no: The ascending pattern is called 'aaroha'. The descending is 'avroha'.

hints: For the skip from Sa to Ga, lift two fingers at once - practise this move on its own first.
The jump from Ga to Pa is just one more finger. Listen for the interval locking in.
Take your time. Speed comes later; clarity comes first.
